examples.ko: 우리 회사는 업무 분업화가 잘 되어 있어요.
examples.en: Our company has a well-organized division of labor.
Thanks to the division of labor, the work got much faster.
Division of labor is very important in a factory.

examples.ko: 지나친 분업화는 오히려 문제가 될 수 있어요.
examples.en: Too much specialization can actually become a problem.

examples.ko: 요즘은 작업의 분업화를 줄이는 팀도 있어요.
examples.en: These days some teams are reducing the division of tasks.
The higher the level of specialization, the simpler each job becomes.

explain: '분업'이 일을 나눠서 하는 것 자체라면, '분업화'는 그렇게 나뉘어 가는 과정이나 정도를 말할 때 많이 써요. 회사, 공장, 산업 이야기에서 자주 나와요. 반대로 합치는 쪽은 '통합'이라고 해요.
explain_en: If '분업' is the act of splitting up work, '분업화' is used more for the process or degree of that splitting. It often comes up when talking about companies, factories and industries. The opposite direction is '통합' (integration).

examples.en: The team members divided up the work and finished quickly.
If you divide up the work, mistakes decrease.
This shop splits ordering and packing between different people.
Dividing up the tasks is harder than I thought.
How about we divide up the cleaning too?
After we divided up the work, efficiency went up.

explain: 일상에서는 '일을 나눠서 하다'라고 더 자주 말하고, '분업화하다'는 회사나 공장 같은 조직 이야기에서 써요. '일을 분업화하다'처럼 '을/를'과 함께 써요. 반대로 합치는 쪽은 '통합하다'예요.
explain_en: In daily talk people more often say '일을 나눠서 하다', while '분업화하다' fits talk about organizations such as companies and factories. It takes an object, as in '일을 분업화하다'. The opposite direction is '통합하다' (to integrate).

examples.en: The actor is putting on makeup in the dressing room.
I sent flowers to the dressing room before the show.
The dressing room is behind the stage.
I knocked on the dressing room door and went in.
The singer is practicing a song inside the dressing room.

examples.ko: 분장실이 좁아서 여러 명이 함께 써요.
examples.en: The dressing room is small, so several people share it.

explain: 연극, 방송, 공연에서 배우나 가수가 분장하고 옷을 갈아입는 곳이에요. 가게의 '탈의실'이나 '피팅룸'과는 달라요. 방송국에서는 '대기실'이라는 말도 같이 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is the place where actors and singers do their makeup and change in theater, TV and concerts. It is different from a shop's '탈의실' or '피팅룸'. At TV stations people also often say '대기실' (waiting room).

examples.en: My grandfather grows bonsai on the balcony.

examples.ko: 이 분재는 십 년 넘게 길렀어요.
examples.en: I have raised this bonsai for over ten years.
I went to a bonsai exhibition.

examples.ko: 분재에는 물을 너무 많이 주면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You shouldn't give a bonsai too much water.
A friend gave me a small bonsai as a gift.

examples.ko: 분재가 마치 큰 나무를 줄여 놓은 것 같아요.
examples.en: The bonsai looks like a big tree made small.

explain: 화분에 나무를 작게 가꾸는 일이나 그 나무를 말해요. 보통 '분재를 키우다', '분재를 가꾸다'처럼 말해요. 그냥 '화분'이나 '화초'와는 달라서 나무 모양을 다듬는 느낌이 있어요.
explain_en: It refers to growing a tree small in a pot, or to that tree itself. People usually say '분재를 키우다' or '분재를 가꾸다'. It differs from plain '화분' or '화초' because it carries the sense of shaping the tree.

examples.en: The family has been moving around busily since morning.

examples.ko: 직원들이 손님 맞을 준비로 분주히 일해요.
examples.en: The staff are busily working to get ready for the guests.
People in the market come and go busily.

examples.ko: 그는 발표 준비를 하느라 분주히 뛰어다녔어요.
examples.en: He ran around busily preparing for the presentation.

examples.ko: 명절 전날 부엌에서는 모두 분주히 음식을 만들어요.
examples.en: The day before the holiday, everyone in the kitchen is busily cooking.
People are walking hurriedly through the airport.

explain: '바쁘게'보다 이리저리 서두르며 움직이는 모습이 잘 보일 때 써요. 보통 '분주히 움직이다', '분주히 오가다'처럼 몸이 움직이는 말과 같이 나와요. 형용사는 '분주하다'예요.
explain_en: Compared with '바쁘게', it fits when you can picture people hurrying around here and there. It usually pairs with words of movement, as in '분주히 움직이다' or '분주히 오가다'. The adjective is '분주하다'.

examples.en: The child snapped a branch just for fun.
You must not snap the chopsticks.
I got angry and snapped the pencil.
We snapped off branches and made a fire.
We broke the cookie in half and shared it.
Please don't snap that stick.

explain: '부러뜨리다'와 비슷한데 손으로 힘을 줘서 뚝 꺾는 느낌이 더 강해요. 가늘고 긴 것에 주로 써요. '르' 불규칙이라서 '분질러요', '분질렀어요'가 돼요.
explain_en: It is close to '부러뜨리다' but feels more like snapping something off sharply with your hands, usually something thin and long. It is a '르' irregular verb, so it becomes '분질러요' and '분질렀어요'.

examples.en: A lot of dust blows around at the construction site.
I have to wear a mask because of the dust.
They installed a device to reduce dust in the workplace.

examples.ko: 분진에 오래 노출되면 폐에 안 좋아요.
examples.en: Long exposure to dust is bad for the lungs.
I vacuumed up the dust in the room.

examples.ko: 분진은 눈에 잘 안 보여도 건강에 영향을 줘요.
examples.en: Even if dust is hard to see, it affects your health.

explain: 집에서는 보통 '먼지'라고 하고, '분진'은 공사장, 공장, 광산처럼 작업 환경에서 날리는 가루 먼지를 말할 때 많이 써요. 뉴스나 안전 안내문에 자주 나와요. '미세먼지'와 같은 말은 아니에요.
explain_en: At home people just say '먼지', while '분진' is used more for powdery dust in work settings such as construction sites, factories and mines. It often appears in news and safety notices. It is not the same word as '미세먼지' (fine dust).

examples.en: He made exercise his outlet for stress.
Smoke is rising from the volcano's vent.
Children need an outlet to spend their energy.
Writing is the outlet for my feelings.
It is dangerous to block the vent where the gas comes out.

examples.ko: 분출구 없이 화를 참기만 하면 병이 나요.
examples.en: If you only hold in your anger with no outlet, you will get sick.

explain: 가스나 용암이 나오는 구멍을 뜻하기도 하지만, 말할 때는 '감정의 분출구', '스트레스의 분출구'처럼 쌓인 마음을 풀 수 있는 방법이나 곳으로 많이 써요. 보통 '분출구가 필요하다', '분출구를 찾다'로 말해요.
explain_en: It can mean a hole where gas or lava comes out, but in conversation it is mostly used as in '감정의 분출구' or '스트레스의 분출구', meaning a way or place to let out built-up feelings. Common patterns are '분출구가 필요하다' and '분출구를 찾다'.

examples.en: I was furious when I heard the lie.

examples.ko: 분통을 참느라 한참 말을 못 했어요.
examples.en: I couldn't speak for a while because I was holding in my anger.
This is really infuriating.
When I hear that story, my anger surges.
It's no use blowing up in anger.
After waiting and waiting, only my frustration piled up.

explain: 억울하고 분해서 화가 치미는 마음을 말해요. 거의 '분통이 터지다'로 쓰고, '분통을 터뜨리다'는 그 화를 밖으로 드러낸다는 뜻이에요. '화'보다 억울함이 섞인 느낌이 강해요.

phrases.example: 버스가 또 안 와서 분통이 터져요.
phrases.en: The bus didn't come again and I'm fuming.
phrases.nuance_ko: 억울하거나 답답한 일 때문에 화를 참기 힘들 때 써요. 화가 안에서 터져 나온다는 비유예요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when you can hardly hold back anger caused by something unfair or frustrating. It is a figure of speech about anger bursting out.

explain_en: It describes the angry feeling that surges when you feel wronged or resentful. It almost always appears as '분통이 터지다', and '분통을 터뜨리다' means to let that anger out. Compared with plain '화', it carries more of a sense of unfairness.

examples.ko: 우리 팀이 한 점 차로 분패했어요.
examples.en: Our team lost by just one point.
It was a pity that we lost narrowly in the final.
Even if we lose narrowly, let's do our best to the end.
The fans comforted the player who lost so narrowly.
I'm worried we might lose a close one again.
I practiced hard so as not to lose narrowly this time.

explain: 그냥 '지다'보다 아깝고 분한 마음이 담겨 있어서, 점수 차가 작거나 거의 이길 뻔한 경기에 써요. 스포츠 뉴스에 자주 나와요. 반대로 이기는 쪽은 '승리하다', '이기다'라고 해요.
explain_en: Unlike plain '지다', it carries a feeling of regret and frustration, so it fits games lost by a small margin or almost won. It often appears in sports news. The opposite is '승리하다' or '이기다'.

examples.ko: 인구 분포도를 보면 서울에 사람이 많아요.
examples.en: On the population distribution map, Seoul has a lot of people.

examples.ko: 이 분포도에서 빨간색이 가장 많은 지역이에요.
examples.en: This is the area with the most red on this distribution map.
I marked the distribution of the plants on a map.
A distribution chart is easy to read at a glance.
I'm going to put the distribution chart in my presentation.

examples.ko: 점수 분포도가 두 개의 산처럼 나왔어요.
examples.en: The score distribution came out like two mountains.

explain: 어떤 것이 어디에, 얼마나 퍼져 있는지 그림이나 지도로 나타낸 거예요. 인구, 식물, 점수 같은 자료에 써요. 그냥 '분포'는 퍼져 있는 상태 자체를 말하니 '분포도'와 구분해서 써요.
explain_en: It is a picture or map showing where something is spread and how much. It is used for data such as population, plants and scores. '분포' alone refers to the spread itself, so keep it separate from '분포도'.

examples.en: Don't take your anger out on your family just because you're upset.

examples.ko: 그는 힘든 일을 당하면 애꿎은 물건에 분풀이해요.
examples.en: When something hard happens, he takes it out on innocent objects.
I felt sorry for taking it out on my younger sibling.
Some people let off steam by playing games.
I had nowhere to vent, so I walked alone.
Who are you trying to take it out on by saying that?

explain: '화풀이하다'와 거의 같게 써요. 보통 화가 난 원인과 상관없는 사람이나 물건에게 화를 쏟을 때 '에게/한테 분풀이하다'로 말해요. '분풀이를 하다'처럼 명사로도 써요.
explain_en: It is used almost the same as '화풀이하다'. Typically you take anger out on a person or thing unrelated to its cause, as in '에게/한테 분풀이하다'. It can also be used as a noun, as in '분풀이를 하다'.

examples.en: Water is indispensable to life.
Exercise is an indispensable habit for your health.
I threw away the things that weren't essential.
I think mobile phones are indispensable for modern people.
I want to become an indispensable person at my company.

examples.ko: 이 부품은 기계에 불가결해서 꼭 있어야 해요.
examples.en: This part is indispensable to the machine, so it must be there.

explain: 주로 '필수불가결하다'라는 형태로 많이 쓰고, 뉴스나 글에서 자주 나와요. 말할 때는 '꼭 필요하다'가 더 자연스러워요. '없어서는 안 되는'과 같은 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It is most often used in the form '필수불가결하다' and appears often in news and writing. In speech, '꼭 필요하다' sounds more natural. It feels like 'cannot be done without'.

examples.en: The report explained why a price increase is unavoidable.
We debated how unavoidable that policy was.
Even if we accept that it was unavoidable, the problem remains.
The inevitability of restructuring was stressed at the meeting.
Everyone knows that change is inevitable.

examples.ko: 사장님은 이번 결정의 불가피성을 직원들에게 말했어요.
examples.en: The boss told the staff why this decision could not be avoided.

explain: '불가피하다'는 일상에서도 쓰지만 '불가피성'은 주로 회의, 보고서, 토론에서 '왜 어쩔 수 없었는지'를 설명할 때 나와요. 보통 '불가피성을 설명하다/강조하다/인정하다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: '불가피하다' is used in daily life too, but '불가피성' mostly appears in meetings, reports and debates when explaining why something could not be helped. Common patterns are '불가피성을 설명하다/강조하다/인정하다'.

examples.ko: 그는 거짓말을 듣고 불같이 화를 냈어요.
examples.en: He flew into a rage when he heard the lie.
The two of them loved each other with burning passion.
I was shocked because my father got furiously angry.
It was hard to hold back the anger that flared up.
My teacher has a fiery, impatient temper.
The rumor spread like wildfire.

explain: '불같이 화를 내다', '불같이 퍼지다'처럼 감정이나 소문이 세고 빠르게 번질 때 써요. 영어의 'like wildfire'와 비슷할 때가 있어요. 성격을 말할 때는 '불같이'보다 '불같은 성격'이 훨씬 자연스러워요.
explain_en: It is used for strong, fast-spreading feelings or rumors, as in '불같이 화를 내다' and '불같이 퍼지다'. Sometimes it matches English 'like wildfire'. For personality, '불같은 성격' is much more natural than '불같이'.

examples.en: I got bitten by red ants in the mountains and it hurt a lot.

examples.ko: 불개미가 집 앞 화단에 줄지어 다녀요.
examples.en: Red ants are walking in a line in the flower bed in front of my house.

examples.ko: 불개미는 나무 밑에 집을 짓고 살아요.
examples.en: Red ants build nests under trees and live there.
If a red ant bites you, it stings and swells.
I was startled to see a swarm of red ants.
I sprayed insecticide to get rid of the red ants.

explain: 붉은빛이 나는 개미를 말하고, 물리면 따끔해서 조심하라는 이야기에 자주 나와요. 뉴스에서는 외국에서 들어온 '붉은불개미'라는 이름으로 많이 나와요.
explain_en: It refers to reddish ants, and comes up often when people warn that their bite stings. In the news it often appears under the name '붉은불개미' for the red imported fire ant.

en: come to the surface; break out; bulge

examples.en: A problem suddenly came to the surface during the meeting.
When the controversy broke out, the company apologized.
I worry every time suspicions come up.
It was recently that the conflict came into the open.

examples.ko: 작은 오해가 큰 문제로 불거지기도 해요.
examples.en: A small misunderstanding can sometimes blow up into a big problem.

examples.ko: 뉴스에서 새로운 문제가 불거져서 사람들이 놀랐어요.
examples.en: A new problem surfaced in the news and people were surprised.

explain: 문제, 논란, 갈등, 의혹처럼 속에 있던 일이 겉으로 드러나 커질 때 써요. 단순히 '생기다'보다 눈에 띄게 터져 나오는 느낌이에요. 뉴스에서 '논란이 불거지다'로 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It is used when something that was inside, such as a problem, controversy, conflict or suspicion, comes out into the open and grows. Compared with simple '생기다', it feels more like something visibly bursting out. In the news, '논란이 불거지다' is very common.

examples.en: People came out onto the street to watch the fire.
In the old days, people would sometimes crowd over to watch a fire.
Don't look on like a bystander just because it's someone else's problem.

examples.ko: 불구경하는 사람들 때문에 소방차가 못 지나갔어요.
examples.en: The fire truck couldn't get through because of people watching the fire.
It's dangerous, so don't stand and watch the fire. Move far away.
While watching the fire, I saw the firefighters arrive.

explain: 불이 난 것을 구경한다는 말인데, 지금은 '불구경하듯'처럼 남의 어려움을 가만히 보기만 하는 태도를 비유할 때도 많이 써요. 이때는 조금 차갑게 들릴 수 있어요. 실제 화재 때는 위험하니 하지 말라는 말과 함께 나오기도 해요.

phrases.example: 친구가 힘든데 강 건너 불구경하듯 보고만 있었어요.
phrases.en: My friend was struggling and I just stood by watching as if it had nothing to do with me.
phrases.nuance_ko: 자기와 상관없는 일이라 도와주지 않고 가만히 지켜보는 태도를 비판할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to criticize a person who watches without helping because they treat it as none of their business.

explain_en: It means to watch a fire, but nowadays people often use '불구경하듯' figuratively for just watching someone else's trouble without helping. In that use it can sound a bit cold. For real fires it often comes up in warnings not to do it because it is dangerous.
